chunks: A group of my scholars, among them 'Ali ibn al-Husayn and Muhammad ibn al-Hasan, narrated to me from Sa'd, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad and Muhammad ibn al-Husayn and Ibrahim ibn Hashim, all from al-Hasan ibn 'Ali ibn Faddal, from Abi Jamilah al-Mufaddal ibn Salih, from Shihab ibn 'Abd Rabbih, from Abi 'Abdillah (peace be upon him), that he said:

When al-Husayn ibn 'Ali (peace be upon him) ascended 'Aqabat al-Batn, he said to his companions, 'I see nothing for myself but being killed.' They said, 'Why is that, O Aba 'Abdillah?' He said, 'A vision I saw in my sleep.' They said, 'What is it?' He said, 'I saw dogs biting me, and the harshest of them upon me was a spotted dog.'

key_terms.أَبْقَعُ: Spotted or speckled, referring to the specific dog in the vision.
key_terms.الْمَنَامِ: Sleep or the state of dreaming.
key_terms.عَقَبَةَ الْبَطْنِ: A specific location or pass near Mecca where Imam Husayn paused during his journey.

ai.seo_question: What did Imam Husayn see in his dream that foretold his martyrdom?
ai.summary: This narration from *Kamil al-Ziyarat* highlights Imam al-Husayn’s (a.s.) spiritual foresight as he ascends 'Aqabat al-Batn, interpreting a prophetic dream of being devoured by dogs—specifically a spotted one—as a prelude to his martyrdom. In Shia tradition, this vision is often linked to the specific manner of his death and the betrayal he faced, serving as a key moment of acceptance (rida) before the Battle of Karbala. The chain of transmission underscores the reliability of the Qummi school in preserving these eschatological and historical details regarding the Ahl al-Bayt.
